idiom_name: large-message-destinations + maximum-large-frame-size (file-backed spill, id on the wire)
implementation_notes: Akka's remoting layer already implements the pattern for configured destinations: actor paths listed in the large-message stream configuration receive payloads above maximum-large-frame-size spilled to a file on the sender side, with only a reference travelling in the remoting frame, so no application-level Check Luggage is needed. It protects the transport (and the frame limit) rather than the JVM heap - the receiving node still materialises the payload - so it is the right default when the problem is message size, not consumer memory.
pitfalls: Large-message destinations are configured per actor path: a new actor that receives big payloads but was not added silently sends them inline and hits the frame limit.
The spill file is an implementation detail of the remoting layer, so it cannot be redeemed by a non-Akka consumer - a claim check meant to outlive the actor system needs a real store.
The receiver still allocates the full payload, so a node short on heap fails even though the transport handled the message.

variants.name: StreamRefs: hand the consumer a stream handle instead of the data
variants.implementation_notes: StreamRefs sends a SourceRef/SinkRef - a serializable handle to a live stream - so the payload is pulled over a side channel with backpressure instead of being pushed in a message; the reference is the claim check and the side channel is the store. Choose it when the consumer should control the transfer rate or when the data is too large to materialise at once, and accept that the reference is bound to a live stream that times out if it is never materialised.
variants.code_sketch:
// sender: hand over a handle, not the bytes
val ref: Future[SourceRef[ByteString]] =
  Source(chunks).runWith(StreamRefs.sourceRef())
ingest ! PayloadRef(ref)      // consumer materialises the stream on demand
pitfalls: A stream reference is only valid while both sides are alive and the stream materialises: if the receiver ignores or cancels it, the data is silently gone and the sender must have a fallback.
StreamRefs is not durable - a node restart loses the stream, so anything that must survive a redeploy belongs in an external store.
Backpressure is the point, but it also means one slow consumer holds a live stream on the producer, which is a resource the producer must bound.
